a: through Malachi
p: The Hebrew has the name or title 'Malachi'. The Greek reads 'by the hand of his messenger' and adds a call to take it to heart.

readings.en: by the hand of Malachi
readings.plain: through Malachi

readings.en: by the hand of his messenger
readings.plain: through his messenger

why: The Hebrew has no pronoun ('his') and the same word is used as a name in later tradition. The Greek translators read the word as a title, 'messenger', and added 'his'. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew name and puts the title in the note.
b: The Greek verse also ends with an addition: 'Set it on your hearts' (thesthe de epi tas kardias hymon), which has no counterpart in the Hebrew. It echoes the 'take to heart' of Haggai 1:5 and Malachi 2:2. No Dead Sea scroll in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription preserves 1:1.

a: the jackals of the wilderness
p: The Hebrew has a rare plural meaning jackals. The Greek has a word for gifts.

readings.en: for jackals of the wilderness
readings.plain: the jackals of the wilderness

readings.en: for gifts of the wilderness
readings.plain: gifts of the wilderness

why: The Hebrew word tannot (jackals) fits the ruin images in Isaiah 34:13 and Jeremiah 49:33. The Greek translator probably did not know the rare plural and read it as a word for gifts; that is a guess.

a: I made his mountains a waste
p: The Hebrew has 'his mountains'. The Greek has 'his borders'.

readings.en: and I made his mountains a desolation
readings.plain: I made his mountains a waste

readings.orig: καὶ ἔταξα τὰ ὅρια αὐτοῦ εἰς ἀφανισμόν
readings.en: and I set his borders for destruction
readings.plain: I set his borders for destruction

why: The Hebrew harav, 'his mountains', fits Edom's hill country (Obadiah 1:8-9). The Greek horia is the word it also uses for 'territory' in 1:4 and 1:5, so the translator may have rendered freely, or read another word; I cannot tell which.

a: turn up your nose at it
t: At it, at me, or I blew on them?
p: The Hebrew has 'you puff at it'. A scribal tradition says 'at me'. The Greek has the LORD blowing.

readings.en: and you puff at it
readings.plain: turn up your nose at it

readings.w: Tiqqune Sopherim tradition (a tradition about the text, not a manuscript)
readings.en: and you puff at me
readings.plain: and you turn up your nose at me

readings.en: and I blew on them
readings.plain: and I blew them away

why: The Hebrew as we have it makes sense: the people scorn the offering. The Greek has the LORD as the one who blows, after a first clause 'these things come from hardship'. The tradition that the original said 'at me' is not backed by a manuscript. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.
b: See the note at 1:13 on the Tiqqune Sopherim.

a: I am about to rebuke your offspring
p: The same Hebrew letters, read with different vowels, give 'offspring' or 'arm'. The Greek and Latin chose the arm.

readings.en: rebuking your seed
readings.plain: I am about to rebuke your offspring

readings.en: I will cut off the shoulder from you
readings.plain: I am about to cut off the shoulder from you

readings.en: I will throw the arm at you
readings.plain: I am about to throw the arm at you

why: The Hebrew makes sense as it stands: the LORD rebukes the priests' descendants or their crops (the 'seed'). The Greek and Latin read the same consonants as zero'a, 'arm' or 'shoulder', perhaps the priests' share of the sacrifice (Leviticus 7:32-34), which would then be taken away. Both fit the section on priests' dues.
b: The Hebrew also has go'er, 'rebuking', where the Greek has a verb of setting apart. The Syriac and the Targum are not cited here.

a: and has become the husband of the daughter of a foreign god
t: A foreign god's daughter or foreign gods?
p: The Hebrew says Judah married the daughter of a foreign god. The Greek says Judah loved and pursued foreign gods.

readings.en: and has married the daughter of a foreign god
readings.plain: and has become the husband of the daughter of a foreign god

readings.orig: ἐν οἷς ἠγάπησεν καὶ ἐπετήδευσεν εἰς θεοὺς ἀλλοτρίους
readings.en: in which he delighted, and pursued foreign gods
readings.plain: and has gone after foreign gods

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading and the one the Greek can be explained from: the Greek has turned a vivid and difficult phrase into a general charge of idolatry. 4QXIIa (4Q76) preserves this verse, but the word 'house' that the printout shows is restored in brackets, so it is not cited as a reading. Whether any of its letters are visible on the leather is a question for the editors' text (Fuller, DJD XV); the printout does not settle it.

a: the one who wakes and the one who answers
p: The Hebrew is 'one who wakes and one who answers'. A scroll reads 'witness'. The Greek has 'until he is humbled'.

readings.en: one who wakes and one who answers
readings.plain: the one who wakes and the one who answers

readings.w: 4QXIIa (4Q76), an Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription of a Dead Sea scroll
readings.en: a witness and one who answers
readings.plain: a witness and one who answers

readings.en: until he is humbled
readings.plain: until he is humbled

readings.en: teacher and student
readings.plain: the teacher and the student

why: The Hebrew is hard, but a reading that is hard in this way is likelier than one that smooths it. The scroll's 'ed ('witness') differs only in the last letter (d for r, two letters easily confused) and gives a clear sense, which makes it a possible original. The Greek and Latin are guesses at the same letters.
b: The printout shows the scroll's 'ed without brackets, so the reading is visible on the leather. The rest of the verse is partly restored.

a: You betrayed her, though she is your companion
t: A shorter text in a scroll
p: The Hebrew says 'whom you betrayed' before 'she is your companion'. A scroll goes straight to 'she is your companion'.

readings.orig: אֲשֶׁר אַתָּה בָּגַדְתָּה בָּהּ וְהִיא חֲבֶרְתֶּךָ
readings.en: to whom you were treacherous, though she is your companion
readings.plain: You betrayed her, though she is your companion

readings.w: 4QXIIa (4Q76), an Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription of a Dead Sea scroll
readings.en: and she is your companion
readings.plain: She is your companion

why: The longer text matches the repeated 'betray' of 2:10-16 and is in the Greek too. The scroll is shorter; either a scribe skipped the clause, or the longer reading was added. The scroll is damaged around this line, so the printout cannot rule out a gap in the transcription.

a: Did he not make one?
p: The Hebrew asks if God made one. The Greek asks if he did well. Both are hard.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXIIa (4Q76) in this phrase, partly restored
readings.en: and not one he made
readings.plain: Did he not make one?

readings.en: and did he not do well
readings.plain: Did he not do well?

why: The Hebrew has an unusual verse structure and no certain meaning; the Greek made a smoother sentence by reading a different word for 'one'. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew words and says in the note that the sense is unsure.

a: And what was the one seeking?
p: A scroll and the Greek add 'And you say' before the question, making it one of the people's objections.

readings.en: and what is the one seeking
readings.plain: And what was the one seeking?

readings.w: 4QXIIa (4Q76), an Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription of a Dead Sea scroll; Septuagint (Swete's text)
readings.en: and you say: what is the one seeking
readings.plain: And you say, 'What was the one seeking?'

why: The scroll's added word matches the book's usual 'and you say' (1:2, 6, 7; 2:17; 3:7, 8, 13). The Greek has it too. That is early support, but it could also be a scribe making the verse fit the pattern. The Hebrew without it is the harder text.

a: For he hates sending away, says the LORD, the God of Israel, and covering one's garment with violence
t: Hate divorce, or divorce if you hate?
p: The Hebrew can say the LORD hates divorce. The Greek and the Latin say: if you hate her, send her away. A Dead Sea scroll shows only the first words of that reading.

readings.orig: כִּי־שָׂנֵא שַׁלַּח אָמַר יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכִסָּה חָמָס עַל־לְבוּשׁוֹ
readings.en: for he hates sending away, says the LORD, the God of Israel, and covers violence over his garment
readings.plain: For he hates sending away, says the LORD, the God of Israel, and covering one's garment with violence

readings.w: 4QXIIa (4Q76), an Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription of a Dead Sea scroll: the words visible on the leather
readings.en: but if you hate, send away
readings.plain: If you hate her, send her away

readings.orig: ἀλλὰ ἐὰν μισήσας ἐξαποστείλῃς, λέγει Κύριος ὁ θεὸς τοῦ Ἰσραήλ, καὶ καλύψει ἀσέβεια ἐπὶ τὰ ἐνθυμήματά σου
readings.en: but if you hate and send away, says the LORD, the God of Israel, then ungodliness will cover your thoughts
readings.plain: If you hate her and send her away, says the LORD, the God of Israel, then ungodliness will cover your thoughts

readings.orig: cum odio habueris, dimitte, dicit Dominus Deus Israel; operiet autem iniquitas vestimentum eius
readings.en: when you hate her, send her away, says the LORD God of Israel; but wrongdoing will cover his garment
readings.plain: When you hate her, send her away, says the LORD, the God of Israel; but wrongdoing will cover his garment

why: The three witnesses do not agree on the whole verse. The Hebrew consonants sn' shlh can be read 'he hates sending away' (the Plain English Translation), 'I hate sending away', or 'the one who hates sends away', so the Hebrew is not decisive. The Greek and the Vulgate agree on a conditional, 'if/when you hate, send away', and differ in the second half. Of the scroll, only 'if', 'you hated' and 'send away' ('im, shnth, shlh) are visible; the 'cover' verb is marked as differing in its vowel letters (it begins with yod and ends with waw, where the Masoretic Text has waw and he), and the words 'my garment' and 'says' are restored, so the scroll cannot be cited for the Greek's or the Latin's second half. Russell Fuller, who edited the scroll (DJD XV), wrote an article on the text of this passage (JBL 1991). The scroll, Greek and Latin are early witnesses, but only the scroll is a Hebrew one. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; the note lists all the readings.
b: Rashi and the Targum Jonathan also read 'if you hate her, send her away', and Rashi sends the reader to the dispute in Gittin 90b; the Talmud (Gittin 90a-b) records both ways of reading the line. The consonants sn' can also be read 'I hate', which several modern translations adopt; that is a choice of vowels, not a different manuscript. Matthew 19:3-9 and Mark 10:2-12 are on this site and are the New Testament side of the question.

a: Look, I am about to send my messenger
p: A scroll begins this verse with 'therefore', tying it to the question of 2:17.

readings.en: here I am sending my messenger
readings.plain: Look, I am about to send my messenger

readings.w: 4QXIIa (4Q76), an Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription of a Dead Sea scroll
readings.en: therefore here I am sending my messenger
readings.plain: Therefore, look, I am about to send my messenger

why: The scroll's 'therefore' is a small connecting word and makes the answer to 2:17 explicit. It may be an addition by a scribe who saw the link, or the original. The Hebrew without it is the shorter text and is in the later witnesses.

a: live through the day he comes
t: A word the scroll seems to lack
p: The printout shows a Dead Sea scroll with a different word where the Hebrew has 'the day of'.

readings.en: and who can sustain the day of his coming
readings.plain: live through the day he comes

readings.w: 4QXIIa (4Q76), an Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription of a Dead Sea scroll
readings.en: who can endure 'otam (them?), their/his coming

why: Where the Masoretic Text has 'et yom, 'the day of', the printout shows the scroll with 'otam, 'them', and a different spelling of 'his coming'. If the scroll really lacks 'day', the sense changes slightly; but this is my reading of a transcription, not the editors', and the text is damaged enough that I do not follow it. The Greek has 'the day of his entry', like the Hebrew.

a: have not come to an end
t: 'Have not come to an end' or 'do not keep away'?
p: The Greek ends 3:6 at 'I do not change' and begins 3:7 with 'you do not keep away from the wrongs of your fathers'. The Hebrew says the sons of Jacob 'have not come to an end'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXIIa (4Q76) and 4QXIIc (4Q78), in the words visible
readings.en: and you, sons of Jacob, have not come to an end
readings.plain: have not come to an end

readings.orig: καὶ ὑμεῖς, υἱοὶ Ἰακώβ, οὐκ ἀπέχεσθε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀδικιῶν τῶν πατέρων ὑμῶν
readings.en: and you, sons of Jacob, do not keep away from the wrongs of your fathers
readings.plain: And you, sons of Jacob, do not keep away from the wrongs of your fathers.

why: A reader with the Greek in front of them gets the opposite sense: in the Hebrew the sons of Jacob survive because the LORD does not change; in the Greek they are blamed for not leaving their fathers' wrongs. I do not know how the Greek translator understood the Hebrew verb. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew, which the scrolls support where they are visible.
b: 4QXIIa shows the verb klythm in 3:6 and 'from the days of your fathers, you turned aside from my statute' in 3:7 as in the Masoretic Text, with ya'aqov spelled with a waw. 4QXIIc (4Q78), which preserves parts of 3:6-7, shows ya'aqov in 3:6 and mechuqqay ('from my statutes') and shemartem ('you kept') in 3:7, also as the Masoretic Text; its other words in these lines are restored and not cited. In 3:7 4QXIIa has the singular wa'amarta ('and you say') where the Masoretic Text has the plural.

a: Can a person rob God?
p: The Hebrew verb means rob. The Greek has the verb used of Jacob's supplanting his brother.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXIIa (4Q76), reading the same word
readings.en: will a person rob God
readings.plain: Can a person rob God?

readings.en: will a person trip up God
readings.plain: Can a person trip up God?

why: The verb qava' is rare and was misread or paraphrased in antiquity. The Greek pternizō is the verb of Genesis 27:36, 'to supplant, to trip up'. Rob suits the context (tithes withheld); the Greek may reflect an old word play on Jacob (see the note).
b: 4QXIIa preserves this verse and agrees with the Masoretic Text in the word. The Greek verse 3:9-10 differs widely from the Hebrew.

a: the proud and everyone who does evil
p: The Hebrew has 'the proud'. The Greek has 'foreigners'.

readings.en: all the proud
readings.plain: the proud and everyone who does evil

readings.en: all the foreigners
readings.plain: the foreigners and everyone who does evil

why: The Greek has 'foreign' for the Hebrew zedim ('proud') here and at 3:15, where 4QXIIa visibly reads zdym, so the scroll supports the Hebrew. The Greek translator probably read zarim ('strangers'), since dalet and resh are easily confused; that is a guess. The Hebrew fits 3:15, where the people call 'the proud' happy. The scroll's 4:1 word is restored and not cited.

a: calves released from the stall
p: The Hebrew has 'stall' (fattening pen). The Greek has 'bonds'.

readings.en: like calves of the stall
readings.plain: calves released from the stall

readings.en: like calves loosed from bonds
readings.plain: calves released from their bonds

why: The Hebrew marbeq (stall or fattening pen) is used for well-fed calves in Amos 6:4. The Greek 'loosed from bonds' is a free rendering of the same picture of freedom. The sense is the same: joy at being let out.

a: you will trample the wicked
t: A different letter in the scroll
p: The printout shows a different consonant in the verb 'trample'.

readings.en: and you will trample the wicked
readings.plain: you will trample the wicked

readings.w: 4QXIIa (4Q76), an Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription of a Dead Sea scroll
readings.en: (the verb is spelled with tsade where the Masoretic Text has samekh)

why: The printout marks the scroll's verb as differing from the Masoretic Text by a consonant, not only by a vowel letter. The two sibilants can interchange in spelling, and the sense 'trample' or 'crush' is probably the same, but I cannot tell from a transcription whether the scribe meant another verb. The Greek has 'trample' (katapatesete), like the Hebrew.
b: Other differences the printout marks in 4QXIIa are spelling-level or tiny: 2:13 me'on for me'ayin; 2:17 'osey for 'oseh; 3:10 bzwt for bzt, and an added object marker before 'the blessing'. None changes the sense.

a: Remember the law of Moses my servant. At Horeb I gave him commands for all Israel, rules and rulings.
p: In the Hebrew the call to remember Moses comes first. In the Greek it comes last. This entry and the one on 4:6 go together.

readings.en: remember the law of Moses my servant
readings.plain: Remember the law of Moses my servant. At Horeb I gave him commands for all Israel, rules and rulings.

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text), where this verse comes last, after the Elijah verses
readings.orig: μνήσθητε νόμου Μωσῆ τοῦ δούλου μου
readings.en: remember the law of Moses my servant (as the last verse of the book)

why: The Hebrew order puts Moses first, then Elijah and the final threat. The Greek order ends the book on Moses, so the last words are 'rules and rulings' and not 'ban'. Which order is older is uncertain; the Hebrew order is the order of the Masoretic Text and the medieval Hebrew manuscripts, and gives the book its stern ending, which Jewish reading practice later softened by repeating 4:5.
b: The printout lists the scroll's text verse by verse, so it cannot show the order of the verses on the leather; the scroll is not cited for either order.

a: Elijah the prophet
t: Elijah the prophet, or the Tishbite?
p: The Greek adds a name: Elijah the Tishbite, the title of 1 Kings 17:1.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4QXIIa (4Q76), which spells the name with a final waw (אליהו)
readings.en: Elijah the prophet
readings.plain: Elijah the prophet

readings.en: Elijah the Tishbite
readings.plain: Elijah the Tishbite

why: The Hebrew has the shorter and more general title; the Greek supplied the full name from 1 Kings 17:1. The scroll's longer spelling of the name is a spelling difference only.

a: the great and awesome day
p: The Hebrew has 'awesome'. The Greek has a word meaning 'manifest' or 'notable'.

readings.en: the great and awesome
readings.plain: the great and awesome day

readings.en: the great and manifest
readings.plain: the great and notable day

why: The Hebrew nora' is the word of Joel 2:31, and the Greek Malachi has the same word as the Greek Joel as Acts 2:20 quotes it (epiphane). The Greek may have been influenced by that verse, or the translator may have softened 'awesome'; the Hebrew is the likelier original. The scroll's word is restored and not cited.

a: and the hearts of sons back to their fathers
t: Sons to fathers, or a person to his neighbor?
p: The Greek has the heart of a person turned to his neighbor, in place of the sons turned to their fathers.

readings.en: and the heart of sons to their fathers
readings.plain: and the hearts of sons back to their fathers

readings.orig: καὶ καρδίαν ἀνθρώπου πρὸς τὸν πλησίον αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and the heart of a person to his neighbor
readings.plain: and the heart of a person back to his neighbor

why: The Hebrew phrase is the same in all Hebrew witnesses. The Greek broadens it, perhaps to make the turning a matter of every kind of neighbor and not only the family; the sense of 'sons' in the Hebrew is the likely original.

a: Otherwise I will come and strike the land and put it under the ban.
t: The last verse and the Greek order (goes with 4:4)
p: The Greek adds the verse on Moses after this one, so the book ends on the law and not on the threat. This entry goes with the one on 4:4.

readings.en: lest I come and strike the land with a ban
readings.plain: Otherwise I will come and strike the land and put it under the ban.

readings.w: Septuagint (Swete's text), where the verse on Moses follows
readings.orig: μὴ ἔλθω καὶ πατάξω τὴν γῆν ἄρδην· μνήσθητε νόμου Μωσῆ
readings.en: lest I come and strike the land utterly. Remember the law of Moses...
readings.plain: Otherwise I will come and strike the land and put it under the ban. Remember the law of Moses my servant. At Horeb I gave him commands for all Israel, rules and rulings.

why: See 4:4. The Greek 'utterly' (ardēn) renders the Hebrew cherem. The Hebrew order ends the book on the threat, a fact that explains why the Jewish reading practice repeats 4:5.

a: He will turn the hearts of fathers back to their sons
p: The Greek verb is 'will restore', and the first noun is singular: the heart of a father to a son.

readings.en: and he will turn back the heart of fathers to sons
readings.plain: He will turn the hearts of fathers back to their sons

readings.orig: ὃς ἀποκαταστήσει καρδίαν πατρὸς πρὸς υἱόν
readings.en: who will restore the heart of a father to a son
readings.plain: He will restore the heart of a father to a son

why: The Greek verb apokatastesei is the verb of Matthew 17:11, where Jesus says that Elijah 'will restore all things', so the Greek Malachi is part of the background of that saying. Sirach 48:10 says that Elijah will 'restore the tribes of Jacob' (with a related verb), and Luke 1:17 follows the Hebrew 'turn' (epistrepsai) with plural hearts, not the Greek's singular 'restore'. The Hebrew heshiv can also mean 'restore', so the Greek is a fair rendering; the Plain English Translation keeps 'turn' for the Hebrew and the note on 4:6 carries the double meaning. The next entry (a person to his neighbor) is the other Greek difference in this verse.
